messages.subject: Re: Problem with mask?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabrielle

In 'secr' the habitat mask may be session-specific, so when the make.mask function is used with a multi-session traps object it returns a list of masks, one per session.

In 'openCR' one habitat mask is used across all sessions (mostly to keep the programming simple).

When you call openCR.fit with a multi-session mask it gives the warning you saw. This is not a worry if the first mask is OK for all sessions; otherwise you may want to specify a mask that relates to the maximum extent of trapping.

I think your problem is more basic: these data are just too thin to support capture-recapture analysis. The number of (female) quolls per year ranged between 1 and 4, and only two quolls were recaptured between years. No way can you expect to estimate year-specific density. I was able to fit a constant-parameter non-spatial model that estimated annual survival = 0.36 (95% CI  0.11-0.72) that is barely informative especially given the usual problems with non-spatial estimates. Perhaps you might want to try constant-parameter spatial models, but don't expect to chart year-year variation with these data.

Murray

P.S. You show the interval between the first and second sessions as 3, but they are numbered consecutively, so I wonder if this is a mistake.

messages.subject: openCR AIC discrepancy between (printed) output of fitted model and AIC() function
messages.subject_clean: openCR AIC discrepancy between (printed) output of fitted model and AIC() function
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

It appears that, in openCR, often the AIC values of the printed model output and the AIC function do not agree perfectly.

Its a minor thing, but I was wondering which AIC value should be trusted more? I guess the AIC from the AIC function? Below is an example what I mean.

Thanks a lot in Advance
Lukas

#openCR-examples _ example
#from page 2 CJS models
library(openCR)

#differing AIC values when using AIC() or directly from printed output

#Example model
model1<-openCR.fit(microtusFMCH, model = list(phi ~ sex+t, p ~ 1))

#AIC when just looking at the output of model1 is AICc = 751.6394
model1

# Analysis type   :  CJS
# Model           :  p~1 phi~sex + t
# Fixed (real)    :  none
# N parameters    :  7
# Log likelihood  :  -368.633
# AIC             :  751.266
# AICc            :  751.6394

#AICc when using AIC() is 753.266
AIC(model1)

#which of the two AIC values should be reported? I guess the one from the AIC function?

messages.subject: Re: openCR AIC discrepancy between (printed) output of fitted model and AIC() function
messages.subject_clean: openCR AIC discrepancy between (printed) output of fitted model and AIC() function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lukas
This is a bit complicated. First, the AIC values are identical, only the AICc values differ. AICc depends on the sample size n, for which there is not strong theory or universal agreement - one reason for preferring AIC as your criterion (there are others).

The difference is because AIC.openCR() has an argument n that defaults to NULL and gives AICc = AIC+2, whereas print.openCR() assumes n = number of different individuals and computes AICc internally - in the Microtus example n = 308 and AICc is close to AIC.

Try AIC(model1, n = 308).

This needs to be tidied up or at least better documented. Thanks for pointing it out.

Murray

messages.subject: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data
messages.subject_clean: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am new to SECR and want to confirm its applicability to my data and sampling method.

I want to calculate sex-specific spatial patterns (mainly density, home range, dispersion) for an arboreal, gliding lizard (Draco dussumieri).

Here’s the sampling details-

I sampled three areca nut plantations (unequal size) with 17 surveys in each plantation.

I surveyed each plantation 1-2 times a week, scanning each tree and noting down GPS coordinates of the tree on which an individual was spotted, along with the sex and ID of that individual.

Each survey was time constrained and I randomized the path taken.

I also took GPS coordinates of all the trees in all three plantations.

Potential caveats-

Some of the edge individuals also utilize forest which I couldn’t sample due to multiple challenges.

In two of the plantations I couldn’t achieve 100% marking so for those two the data is a mix of marked and unmarked. (Considering using SMR model for these two)

I am a bit unsure whether I can use SCR for analysis so posting in this group.

Additionally, in case it can be used, can the trees act as traps (average spacing of trees is 2 to 3 m) or should I adopt the polygon search method?

I also measured perch height of the individuals while sampling so was wondering if the detection probability can be modeled using perch height as a covariate?

I would be really grateful if it could be addressed and also if any further clarifications are required.

Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data
messages.subject_clean: Application of SCR to arboreal lizard data
messages.body_plain:
Hello
This is an interesting study and there's a lot to think about, but you seem to be on the right track.

Edge individuals are accommodated by spatial capture-recapture if you know (can map) the extent of potential habitat outside the study area.

Were lizards marked before you started the surveys? You imply (almost) all individuals were marked. Then it's worth thinking what you want out of spatial capture recapture. Fitting a density surface model allowing for movements?

Whether to use trees as notional 'detectors' is largely a matter of taste and practicality. I would say 'yes' if possible. Often it's easier to discretize polygons rather than use the polygon detector type, but the original Royle & Young 2008 horned lizard dataset is a counter example. GPS error may become an issue.

My feeling is that perch height is useful only if you document the available perch heights (perhaps as a covariate of 'tree'), and maybe not even then. Sex differences in perch height can be analysed outside the capture-recapture analysis.

I hope that others weigh in with their thoughts.

Murray

Hello Cheryl
It's possible you've hit on a blind spot in my coding of modelAverage (a condition I didn't allow for, and that I should fix), but there's some teasing out before I go there.

The result from modelAverage is "an array of model-averaged estimates" - you shouldn't expect predict to work on that.

Your problem seems to be that 'avg' doesn't include all levels of "Treatment". 'newdata' is the way to get that, but I don't see what you have attempted there.

Pushing back on a couple of points. Would you really expect the learned response to differ between treatments (i.e. why not b + Treatment)? Spacing your code would make it more readable.

Murray
